78: Our base is a permitted commissary, and we do not build one. A BBQ caterer cannot legally cook for clients at home, so we rent time in a shared commissary kitchen that already holds the health permit: production hours, cold and dry storage, and a yard or lot where the smoker trailer can be parked and, where the rules allow it, fired. The example budgets {{alquiler_mes}} per month for all of it. Published rates for shared kitchens typically run from $15 to $45 an hour depending on the city and the equipment, according to The Food Corridor, so we compare at least three commissaries on price, on hours that fit a Saturday-heavy schedule, on cooler and freezer space and on how early we can load on event days. Before paying a deposit we sign a written commissary agreement that spells out our hours, our shelves and refrigeration, where the smoker may sit and burn, cleaning duties, insurance requirements and notice for ending the arrangement. Most county health departments want to see it, and so will a lender. The rule we keep is simple: own what travels with you and rent what you use a few days a week. That keeps the investment far below a leased restaurant and lets us add hours in wedding season and cut them in January.
79: The equipment list follows the order in which food moves, so we buy in that order too. First, what cooks: the smoker trailer, an offset or reverse-flow unit in the 500-gallon class ({{inv_vehiculo}}), its upfit with a warming cabinet, storage boxes and lights ({{inv_adaptacion}}), and the live-fire rig for Santa Maria, asado and whole hog cooks ({{inv_rig}}). Second, what holds: insulated food carriers, hot boxes and chafing dishes ({{inv_holding}}). Third, what carries and serves: a used cargo van ({{inv_furgoneta}}) with its shelving and tie-downs ({{inv_furgoneta_upfit}}), plus the carving board, canopy and tables. The tow vehicle is the owner's pickup, so it costs nothing in the plan. If you do not own one rated to pull the trailer, a used pickup is a separate purchase, which we estimate at $25,000 to $40,000 (Kit estimate). Propane is the backup for burn bans, not the main fuel.
80: Every event follows the same six phases, from the quote to the final payment. One, the briefing, about three weeks out, where we confirm the menu style, the guest count, the timeline and the allergies. Two, a venue visit about two weeks out to decide where the trailer or the rig goes, which way the smoke will blow, where water and power are and how far the carving station sits from the buffet. Three, ordering the meat five to seven days ahead. Four, rubs, trimming and portioning in the commissary. Five, the overnight cook: the calculator gives a "Start the pit by" time for the service time you quote, and the pitmaster cooks to the probe, not the clock. Six, resting and hot holding, loading, setup in 60 to 90 minutes, service from the buffet and carving station, then pack-down, cold ash in a metal can and the final invoice with any add-ons. Write the times down for every event; that log is your best defense if a guest ever complains.
81: Food safety in smoked meat starts with knowing which temperature you are talking about. A brisket is done for quality at about 203 °F (95 °C), when the probe slides in with no resistance. That is a taste target, not a safety rule. The safety floors come from the FDA Food Code: 145 °F (63 °C) for intact cuts, 155 °F (68 °C) for injected, tenderized or ground meat and sausage, and 165 °F (74 °C) for poultry. Injecting a brisket or a pork butt makes it non-intact, so the 155 °F floor applies. Hold hot food at 135 °F (57 °C) or above in insulated carriers and hot boxes, and calibrate every probe. Food you cool for later goes from 135 °F to 70 °F (21 °C) within 2 hours and to 41 °F (5 °C) within a total of 6 hours, and you reheat it to 165 °F (74 °C) before holding it again. Plan on a yield of about 50% of the raw weight for brisket and pork butt, according to Dr. BBQ at fieryfoodscentral.com, and write every allergen in the rubs, sauces and sides on the quote.
82: We buy meat from an approved source, which means a USDA-inspected or state-inspected plant, and we keep the invoices. Packer briskets, pork butts and ribs come from a meat purveyor or a cash-and-carry such as Restaurant Depot, whichever gives the better price and the steadier grade; we ask for the same cut and weight every week so the cook times repeat. Wood is a second supply line: post oak in Texas, hickory, and red oak for Santa Maria, plus charcoal and a small stock of pellets. Sides, bread and sauces come from the commissary or a local vendor, and a party rental company covers the tables, linens and chafing fuel we do not own. Keep a maintenance calendar for the smoker, the trailer and the van: grease and ash out after every cook, and tires, brakes, lights and hitch checked before the season.
85: The team is small and every role has a clear job. The owner is the pitmaster, who also sells, buys and runs the pit at the events that matter most. A pit cook or lead cook, a part-time hourly W-2 employee, runs the second shift at the smoker and covers the big events. Event staff (servers, buffet attendants and carvers) are hourly W-2 employees who work event by event, and a prep cook who doubles as the van driver works part time. There is no dining room, no front-of-house manager and no office, so the payroll flexes with the calendar and the events pay for the structure.
86: Labor costs {{personal_a1}} in year 1, which is {{personal_pct}} of sales. That figure includes the owner's pay and the employer payroll taxes for everyone on the payroll. It is the biggest line after the food, and it moves with the calendar: in a May with three weddings and two graduations everyone works, and in February almost nobody does. The owner's pay and the pit cook's pay are fixed, while event staff cost depends on the hours of each event. If you book fewer events than planned, you schedule fewer hours and the cost drops; if you book more, you carry them with the same people until the coverage runs out and then add someone to the payroll, never a contractor who invoices you by the event. Change the "Staffing" sheet to your own wage rates before you show this plan to a lender.
87: Every event takes hours of portioning, overnight cooking, loading, travel, setup, service and breakdown. The workbook assumes {{horas_evento}} hours per person and {{personas_evento}} people per event on average, and it compares the hours scheduled with the hours needed to give a coverage of {{cobertura_horas}}. As a rule of thumb, plan one server or buffet attendant for every 25 to 30 guests at a buffet (Kit estimate); one pit cook can watch several cooks at once, so the pit crew does not grow with the guest count. High coverage does not mean you have too many people. It means the roster can carry the busy Saturdays, including a weekend with two weddings. The workbook spreads payroll evenly over the 12 months, which is conservative.
88: Everyone but the owner is a W-2 employee. Event staff work under our direction, on our schedule and with our equipment, which is the profile the Fair Labor Standards Act treats as employment, and California's AB5 presumes it. Calling them contractors may look cheaper, but misclassification can bring back taxes, penalties and claims, and it can sink a loan application. Payroll taxes add {{cargas_pct}} to wages in the model, workers' compensation is required in nearly every state, and you pay at least the highest of the federal, state and local minimum wage; the workbook uses the federal floor of {{salario_minimo_federal}} for full-time work as its reference, and many states are higher. For wages, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (OEWS, May 2025) puts restaurant cooks at a mean of $18.62 an hour, with the 75th percentile at $21.45, and food servers outside restaurants at $17.37, with the 75th percentile at $18.51. Check your city before you set rates.
89: Training is part of the plan, not an extra. The owner or a lead cook holds a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate such as ServSafe Manager, and every employee who handles food gets the food handler card that your state or county requires. Training covers raw meat, temperatures, cooling and the nine major allergens, because a guest with an allergy has to be able to ask the carver and get the right answer. Add fire and propane safety: where the extinguisher is, how to shut off a tank and how far the canopy sits from the pit. Before the first event of the season, the crew rehearses the script for the carving station and for any live-fire show: when the fire is lit, how the meat is sliced in front of the guests and how each cut is explained. The rehearsal costs a morning and saves you from improvising in front of a hundred guests.
90: Handle the service charge and the gratuity differently, because the IRS does. Under IRS Revenue Ruling 2012-18, a mandatory service charge that the client must pay is treated as wages to the staff who receive it, so payroll taxes apply. A gratuity is voluntary, the amount is the guest's choice and it belongs to the staff. We list them on separate lines of the quote, say plainly what each one pays for and distribute gratuities under a written policy. Check your state's overtime rules too, because a wedding that ends late after an early start is a long shift. Whether the service charge is subject to sales tax depends on your state, which the legal section covers.
93: Taken together, the case describes a small business that is viable on paper. Year-1 sales are {{ventas_a1}}, the gross margin is {{margen_bruto_pct}} and EBITDA is {{ebitda_a1}}, or {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales. The average event brings in {{ventas_evento}}. These are planning figures from the workbook, not a forecast: they hold as long as you book the events in the plan at the average price of the mix. That average includes the corporate drop-offs and the parties, which sell for less, so it is not the price of a wedding. For reference, Q39 in Kansas City lists drop-off at $15 to $30 per person, and a Los Angeles operator lists weddings at $65 to $85. The next sections show where each number comes from.
94: The investment is built from lines you can price today. The largest are the smoker trailer ({{inv_vehiculo}}) and the used cargo van ({{inv_furgoneta}}), followed by the holding and service equipment ({{inv_holding}}), the live-fire rig ({{inv_rig}}), the trailer upfit ({{inv_adaptacion}}), the van upfit ({{inv_furgoneta_upfit}}), the website, photos and first bridal show ({{inv_lanzamiento}}), first-year permits and certifications ({{inv_permisos}}) and the opening inventory ({{inv_stock}}). Startup costs also include a 10% contingency on the trailer, the van and their upfits, and they add up to {{capex}}. On top we set aside working capital of {{fondo_maniobra}}, which covers the first months while payments come in, for a total investment of {{inversion_total}}. The cash needed at opening is {{necesidad_caja}}, funded with {{fondos_propios}} of owner equity and a {{prestamo}} loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, with an annual payment of {{cuota_anual}}. A loan of that size means a bank loan or an SBA 7(a) loan, not a Microloan. The plan is lender-ready, but approval is not guaranteed: the terms are an illustration, not an offer, so get quotes for the trailer and the van before you treat any figure as closed.
95: Revenue grows with the number of events, not with the price. The workbook raises events by {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3, from {{eventos_a1}} to {{eventos_a2}} and then {{eventos_a3}}, at the same price per guest and the same guests per event. That takes sales from {{ventas_a1}} in year 1 to {{ventas_a2}} in year 2 and {{ventas_a3}} in year 3, and net profit from {{resultado_neto_a1}} to {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}. Growth in events is realistic only if repeat business builds: companies that reorder, venues that send you bookings and families that return for the next graduation. The model applies an income tax rate of {{impuesto_beneficios}} as a reserve; with a pass-through LLC the owner pays that tax on a personal return, so keeping the reserve is the prudent choice. Capacity matters too, because one trailer and one crew can only cover so many Saturdays.
96: The cost structure can be checked against reference ranges. Food cost on BBQ package sales is {{coste_paquetes_pct}}, and all goods together are {{cogs_pct}} of sales. Disposables, wood and cooking fuel add {{consumibles_pct}}, because the post oak, charcoal, pellets and propane backup grow with the pounds of meat you cook. Labor is {{personal_pct}} of sales, and the commissary and trailer parking are {{ocupacion_pct}}, or {{ocupacion_anual}} a year. Marketing is {{marketing_anual}} a year, insurance is {{seguros_anual}} and year-1 interest is {{intereses_a1}}. For reference, catering food cost typically runs from 28% to 35% of sales according to Galley Solutions, and net margins from 7% to 8% according to ItsaCheckmate. If your food cost sits above that range, check your yield and your portions first.
97: Break-even is measured in events per year. On an accounting basis the business covers its costs with {{equilibrio_eventos}} events a year. On a cash basis, with loan payments in and depreciation out, it needs {{equilibrio_caja_eventos}}, against {{eventos_a1}} in the plan. That leaves a margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}} over cash break-even: events can fall {{caida_absorbible_pct}} before cash stops covering costs. It is a real cushion, but not a wide one, and a slow spring can eat it. The workbook shows the exact figure and the plan rounds up to whole events. Track it every month.
98: You can fail on cash even when the profit looks good. The workbook assumes you collect from clients in {{cobro_dias}} days on average and pay suppliers in {{pago_dias}} days, with payroll going out every month. The lowest cash balance is {{saldo_minimo}} in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, the lowest debt service coverage is {{dscr_min}} and the payback before debt is {{payback}}. The 50% deposit is not modeled, so real cash should be a little better than the workbook shows.
99: Two scenarios show how fast the numbers move. The pessimistic case assumes {{pesimista_eventos}} events at {{pesimista_invitados}} guests and {{pesimista_precio}} per guest, which gives sales of {{pesimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}. Year-1 closing cash comes out at {{pesimista_caja}}: the cash runs out, and you would need more equity, a credit line or lower spending before you get there. The optimistic case reaches {{optimista_ventas}} with {{optimista_eventos}} events and a pre-tax result of {{optimista_resultado}}. Remember that {{eventos_a1}} events is the pace of a full-time operator with a pit cook, not the average first year. With a thin cushion you have four levers: book more corporate events, adjust the price, add guests per event and negotiate more time with your lender. The workbook rules: if you change a green cell, this document falls behind.
102: You cannot run a BBQ catering business from your home kitchen. The FDA Food Code (section 3-201.11) requires food to come from sources that comply with the law and says that food prepared in a private home may not be used. Cottage food laws do not rescue you: in Texas, the state health department excludes meat, meat products and poultry. California ties catering to a permitted kitchen and does not allow it under its home-kitchen program. That is why this plan smokes in a permitted commissary and signs a written commissary agreement, and why that agreement comes before your business license. This section is general information, not legal advice.
103: With the kitchen secured, the next layer is the local health permit. Expect to apply to your county for a catering or food facility permit, pay an annual fee and pass an inspection of the commissary. At least one person should hold a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate such as ServSafe Manager, and food handlers need the card your state requires. Your written food safety plan is based on HACCP principles and the FDA Food Code: 145 °F (63 °C) for intact meat, 155 °F (68 °C) for injected, tenderized or ground meat and sausage, 165 °F (74 °C) for poultry, hot holding at 135 °F (57 °C) or above, cooling to 70 °F (21 °C) within 2 hours and to 41 °F (5 °C) within a total of 6 hours, and reheating to 165 °F (74 °C). Train on the nine major allergens. Buy only from an approved source: whole hog must come from an inspected plant, because custom-exempt meat is marked not for sale.
104: The permit question gets harder when the smoker trailer cooks at the event. In Texas, a mobile food unit must operate from a central preparation facility or another fixed food establishment, with daily logs, a hand sink, potable water and a certified food manager (25 TAC section 228.221). Florida and North Carolina ask for something similar, and we have not verified California. So ask your county whether smoking or serving from the trailer at the event turns it into a mobile food unit, and which permit that takes. If you cannot get one, smoke in the commissary and bring the meat in hot boxes. Public or community events usually need a temporary food establishment permit, and venues often ask for a certificate of insurance, sometimes naming them as additional insured.
105: Fire rules decide where a pit can burn. The International Fire Code, as your city adopts it, covers solid fuel cooking appliances such as wood-burning BBQ pits. The Corpus Christi Fire Department's bulletin, for example, lists a Class K extinguisher (2.5 gallons, or 9.5 liters) plus a 2A:10BC, 10 feet (3 m) between cooking units and no more than 200 lb (91 kg) of propane. Some cities also ask for a permit for each setup. Burn bans and cooking under tents vary by county and city, so check with your fire marshal before you sign anything. Our contract has a force majeure clause for a burn ban: switch to the propane backup, move the date or cook in the commissary. Keep the extinguisher within reach, keep the pit away from tent walls and put out coals with water into a metal can.
106: Sales tax is where small caterers get surprised. In many states it applies to the whole catering invoice, including food, staff and rentals, and the treatment of a service charge depends on the state: California taxes a mandatory one, and Texas excludes it up to 20% when it is separately stated and paid to qualified employees. Under IRS Revenue Ruling 2012-18, a mandatory service charge is wages, not a tip. Register for a sales tax permit in your state; the workbook applies {{sales_tax}} to the whole invoice, which is the conservative choice. We do not sell alcohol. If the client supplies it, a licensed alcohol service should pour it under its own liquor liability coverage.
107: Hiring and insurance come next. Event staff, the pit cook and the prep cook belong on W-2 payroll with workers' compensation, Form I-9, Form W-4 and your state's new-hire reporting. The FLSA treats servers and carvers as employees in almost every case, and California's AB5 presumes it, so a 1099 is a risk. The example budgets {{seguros_anual}} a year for general liability or a business owner's policy, commercial auto that covers the trailer, workers' compensation and inland marine for the smoker and the equipment in transit. Insureon publishes average prices by policy, so get quotes from an agent who knows caterers, and ask venues for the certificate of insurance and additional insured wording they require before you quote.
108: The last link is the road. The smoker trailer and the van are titled and registered with your state DMV, and trailer rules vary by state, so ask. Your auto policy has to cover commercial use and the trailer. A commercial driver's license is only required at a gross vehicle weight rating of 26,001 lb or more, which a cargo van does not reach. If you operate in the UK, the rules differ: register your food business with the local council at least 28 days before you start trading, even from a mobile unit or temporary premises, expect a Food Hygiene Rating from 0 to 5 (the FHIS in Scotland), keep a HACCP-based plan, declare the 14 listed allergens, charge VAT at 20% on event catering, and agree the event permit and the fire plan with the council and the venue.
111: The plan holds up because of how it is built. There is no restaurant to lease or fit out: the pitmaster smokes in a shared, permitted commissary, the cargo van carries the food hot, and the smoker trailer goes to the event only when the client pays for a live pit on site. Two engines of demand share the calendar, companies that reorder and private clients who book weddings, parties and graduations. The case is viable: sales of {{ventas_a1}}, net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}}, a lowest DSCR of {{dscr_min}} and a payback of {{payback}}. But be honest about the margin. The cushion over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}}, a pace of {{eventos_a1}} events is a full-time operator's, and in the pessimistic case the cash runs out. If volume stalls, you have the levers: more corporate events, price, guests per event and more time with your lender.
112: Know the risks before you sign anything. A late cancellation is handled with the 50% nonrefundable deposit and a cancellation schedule in the contract. A burn ban or rain is handled with a force majeure clause, the propane backup, a new date and a canopy that your fire marshal allows. Meat out of temperature is the risk that can hurt a guest: it is prevented with calibrated probes, hot holding at 135 °F (57 °C) or above, a written HACCP-based plan and liability insurance. A smoker trailer or van breakdown is covered by maintenance, insurance and a backup plan with a rental. A jump in meat prices is handled by reviewing the pricing calculator with your own costs every season. A shortage of staff on peak Saturdays is handled with a bench of trained part-time hourly W-2 employees and early scheduling. Inspections hold no surprises if your permits, logs and commissary agreement are in order. Finally, depending on a few planners and venues for bookings is reduced by direct outreach and repeat clients.
113: Our strengths come from the pit and the carving station. We sell a short list of things and do them in front of the guests, with a pitmaster who explains the meat. The ten menu styles let us fit a wedding, a company or a graduation without reinventing the business, from Texas brisket to Santa Maria tri-tip or an Argentine asado. A permitted commissary and written allergen handling give planners and venues the reassurance they look for. Fixed costs stay low because we share the commissary and run one van, so a slow month hurts less. And our best sales argument is not price. It is the memory of meat cooked low and slow and carved to order, which a grocery tray cannot match.
114: The roadmap follows the six phases of the startup checklist that comes with the kit. "Phase 1 - Business Setup" covers the LLC, the tax registrations, the bank account and the conversation with your lender. "Phase 2 - Pits, Fire & Permits" covers the commissary agreement, the health permit, the food safety plan, the fire rules, the propane backup and the insurance. "Phase 3 - Equipment" covers the smoker trailer, the van, the holding equipment and the supplier network. "Phase 4 - Staff" covers W-2 hiring, schedules and training. "Phase 5 - Marketing" builds the website, the Google Business Profile, the directory listings, the venue and planner outreach and the first tastings. "Phase 6 - First 90 Days" runs the first events and reviews each one against the plan. Do not move to the next phase while the permits of the current one are still open.
115: Measure a few things every week and do not wait for your accountant. Track events booked per month and the share of quotes that become signed contracts. Compare your average price per guest, excluding sales tax, with the {{precio_invitado}} in the plan, remembering that it is an average of the mix and drops with the parties. Track the raw pounds of meat per guest and the real yield of each cut, your food cost against the {{cogs_pct}} in the plan, and the labor hours per event against the workbook. Log cancellations, events where a burn ban or rain changed the plan, and the reviews you collect. Each month, compare your cash balance with the lowest balance in the workbook, {{saldo_minimo}}. If three weeks go by without a signed event, do not wait for the end of the quarter: review your price, your outreach and your calendar.
116: Over three years, the plan is to build a base of clients who come back: weddings by referral, companies that reorder and venues that recommend us. That smooths the calendar and lowers the sales cost of every event, while events grow by {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3. Sales reach {{ventas_a3}} and net profit {{resultado_neto_a3}} in year 3. A second smoker trailer or a full-time pit cook makes sense only when the peak-season calendar is full and you are turning down dates, not before. A restaurant of your own is a different business with different numbers, and it makes sense only if your results ask for it. Meanwhile, growth comes from filling the events you already have more profitably: a higher guest count, better add-ons such as a live pit on site, and more repeat bookings.
117: The next steps are simple, and they go in order. Open the Excel workbook and replace the example figures with yours in the green cells: events per year, price per guest and guests per event. If you change one of them, this document falls behind, so the workbook rules. Use the pricing calculator, with its "Meat Yield & Smoke Schedule" and its "Shopping List by Guest Count", to turn your costs into quotes you can send, and use the checklist so no permit gets skipped. This plan is a planning tool, not legal or tax advice: confirm what applies to you with your accountant, your county health department and your fire marshal. And keep an eye on years 2 and 3, when the loan is being repaid and the cushion over cash break-even matters most.
